```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

Every choice in a pipeline (the recipe, the model, the prompt, the reasoning
effort) changes the answers, and one run on one document cannot say by how
much. A model asked the same question five times can answer it five ways, and
ten questions about one report share that report's quirks, so they are closer
to one observation than to ten. `gr_compare()` shows what each recipe does to
one document and is descriptive only. The functions in this guide answer the
question that follows it: on a labelled set of questions, is configuration A
more accurate than B, by how much, at what cost, and how sure can you be?

The guide follows the order of the work: a reference set and its splits, the
arms to compare and the rule that scores them, a benchmark held to one spending
limit, the report and how to read it, planning the size of a comparison before
running it, judges, baselines that use no model, drift, and the signals the
package records about its own work. The statistics functions underneath come
last. Measuring a screener against people, several reviewers and agreement
between extraction tables are part of a review and are in `vignette("review")`.

## Setting up

Everything below runs offline. `gr_mock_client()` stands in for the model, and
`embedder = "lexical"` keeps retrieval free and deterministic. Two mock model
ids get prices, so the benchmarks below have a cost to compare: `mock-small` at
$0.20 and $0.80 per million input and output tokens, and `mock-large` at ten
times that.

```{r message = FALSE}
library(harnessr)
old <- gr_options(verbose = FALSE, embedder = "lexical")

gr_register_model("mock-small", context_window = 128000, max_output = 4096,
                  input_usd = 0.2, output_usd = 0.8)
gr_register_model("mock-large", context_window = 128000, max_output = 4096,
                  input_usd = 2, output_usd = 8)
```

## References and splits

A reference is the labelled set every configuration is scored on. Each item has
a payload (what the configuration is given), a label (what counts as right),
a cluster and a split. The cluster is the unit whose items share errors,
usually the document: eight questions about one report are not eight
independent observations, and every interval in this guide is computed with
that in mind. `hr_reference()` builds one from any items; `gr_qa_reference()`
builds one of questions about documents, with each question's acceptable
answers:

```{r}
reports <- c(
  north = "The northern region. Revenue was 45.2 million dollars in fiscal 2024. The plant in Leeds made 12,400 units.",
  south = "The southern region. Revenue was 51.8 million dollars in fiscal 2025. Staff numbered 310 at year end.",
  east  = "The eastern region. Revenue was 38.9 million dollars in fiscal 2024. The chair is Ana Ruiz.",
  west  = "The western region. Revenue was 29.4 million dollars in fiscal 2023. Exports rose 7 percent.")

qa <- gr_qa_reference(
  questions = c(n_rev = "What was revenue?", n_units = "How many units did Leeds make?",
                s_rev = "What was revenue?", s_staff = "How many staff were there?",
                e_rev = "What was revenue?", e_ceo = "Who is the chief executive?",
                w_rev = "What was revenue?", w_exp = "By how much did exports rise?"),
  documents = rep(unname(reports), each = 2),
  answers = list("45.2 million", c("12,400", "12400"), "51.8 million", "310",
                 "38.9 million", NA, "29.4 million", "7 percent"),
  unanswerable = "e_ceo",
  cluster = rep(names(reports), each = 2),
  split = "test")
qa
```

The eastern report names a chair and no chief executive, so `e_ceo` is marked
unanswerable: its label is the not-found answer, and a reader is right on it
only when it says the document does not hold the answer. A reference without
such items never tests whether a reader can tell that an answer is missing. An
item
with neither an answer nor the unanswerable flag has no label, and every run on
it is scored `NA`, so it never counts for or against an arm.

Once a benchmark starts scoring a reference, the reference is locked:
`hr_reference_add()` then refuses to add items to it, or to any copy of it,
with an error of class `hr_reference_locked`, so no item can be added after
the results are seen. The reference also carries a SHA-256 hash of
its content, which the benchmark checks.

Splits keep tuning apart from evidence. `dev` is for tuning prompts, settings
and margins, and its scores are never reported. `exploratory` holds early
experiments, `calibration` is for fitting signal thresholds (below), `test` is
what reported comparisons are scored on, and `final`, if used, is held back and
run once per release. `hr_assign_splits()` assigns whole clusters, so no
document has questions on both sides of a tuning and a scoring split:

```{r}
questions <- data.frame(
  item_id  = sprintf("q%03d", 1:120),
  document = rep(sprintf("report%02d.pdf", 1:30), each = 4),
  question = rep(c("What was revenue?", "Who audited the accounts?",
                   "How many staff were there?", "When did the year end?"), 30))
sp <- hr_assign_splits(questions, seed = 2026)
sp
```

The default shares are 10% dev, 10% exploratory, 30% calibration and 50% test.
Each cluster's place comes from the SHA-256 digest of the seed and its id, so
row order and the session's random state do not change it, and with the
default `method = "stable"` adding or dropping a document never moves another.
The price is that the shares are met only on average: 13 of these 30 documents
went to test, not 15. `method = "balanced"` gives each split its share of
whole clusters, at the cost that a document added later can shift others
across a boundary, so draw it once and store it:

```{r}
hr_assign_splits(questions, seed = 2026, method = "balanced")$counts[, c("split", "clusters", "items")]
```

A split given a share that receives no cluster warns with class
`hr_empty_split`, which happens with very few documents.

### Label sheets

Labels come from people. `gr_label_sheet()` writes a CSV with one row per item,
the columns a person needs to judge it and empty columns for their decisions,
with an instructions file beside it. It writes five kinds: `"qa"`,
`"screening"`, `"extraction"`, `"calibration"` and `"judge"`. A blind sheet,
the default, copies only those columns, so a model's answer in `items` stays
out of it:

```{r message = FALSE}
to_label <- head(sp$items, 3)
to_label$model_answer <- c("45.2 million", "Not stated", "310")

path <- file.path(tempdir(), "qa-labels.csv")
sheet <- gr_label_sheet("qa", to_label, path = path)
names(sheet)
```

The person fills `answerable`, `answer` and `quote`. `gr_read_labels()` reads
the sheet back, checks every value and id, and joins the items' other columns
back by `item_id`, renaming one that clashes with a decision column (the
model's `answer` here would come back as `model_answer`):

```{r}
filled <- read.csv(path, fileEncoding = "UTF-8-BOM")
filled$answerable <- c("yes", "no", "yes")
filled$answer <- c("45.2 million dollars", NA, "310")
write.csv(filled, path, row.names = FALSE, na = "")

gr_read_labels(path, "qa", items = to_label)[, c("item_id", "answerable", "answer",
                                                  "split", "model_answer")]
```

A value it cannot read stops it with an error of class `gr_bad_labels` that
names the sheet, the row as a spreadsheet counts it and the item, for every bad
value at once:

```{r}
filled$answer[2] <- "Smith & Co"
write.csv(filled, path, row.names = FALSE, na = "")
tryCatch(gr_read_labels(path, "qa", items = to_label),
         gr_bad_labels = function(e) cat(conditionMessage(e)))
```

With `reviewers = k` each person gets a sheet of their own, so no one sees
another's decisions. `?gr_label_sheet` gives the number of items each kind of
set needs for the package's own evaluation: for question answering, about 480
questions over 88 documents.

## Arms and scorers

An arm is one configuration to compare: a function of an item and a context
that returns the arm's output for that item. `ctx` carries the benchmark's
client, a trace of this run alone, the governor the run is held to and the
run's `draw_index`; `ctx$call()` is `gr_call()` with the client, the trace and
the draw index filled in. Every
request an arm makes has to go through that trace, since it is how the
benchmark counts the run's tokens and dollars and holds it to the limit:

```{r}
ask <- function(name, model) {
  hr_arm(name, function(item, ctx) {
    ctx$call(paste("Item", item), model = ctx$params$model)$text
  }, params = list(model = model))
}
ask("large", "mock-large")
```

The arm records a SHA-256 hash of its name, code, settings and `version`. The
code is hashed as text with the values it names from the environment it was
made in, so the same arm has the same hash in every session and after
`saveRDS()`, and an arm edited after it was built is refused rather than run
under its old name. Change `version` when the arm's behaviour changes.

`gr_arm()` wraps a reading recipe as an arm, and `gr_arms()` builds one per
recipe. Each run reads the item's document with `answer_document()`, or with
`gr_read()` when the document is already chunked, and returns the `gr_answer`.
`settings` takes what `answer_document()` takes in `...`; here they make the
same recipe two arms on two models:

```{r}
arms <- list(gr_arm("fast", settings = list(model = "mock-small"), name = "small"),
             gr_arm("fast", settings = list(model = "mock-large"), name = "large"))
```

A `gr_arm()`'s version is the package version, since readers and prompts change
between releases. Every request of a run, segmenter and reader requests
included, carries the run's draw index. A reader that finds the run's limits
leave it too little room to start returns a partial not-found answer noting the
limit, which is scored as a budget stop rather than an error.

A scorer turns an output and a label into `correct`, an `outcome` (what it
compared) and a `failure_kind` saying why a wrong output was wrong:
`"parse_failure"`, `"refusal"`, `"not_in_document"`, `"wrong"`, `"budget_stop"`
or `"error"`. `hr_scorer_exact()`, the default, compares text after folding case
and white space. `gr_scorer_answer()` is the one for reading recipes: an answer
is right when it contains any acceptable answer, after folding case, white
space and thousands separators, with numbers matched whole:

```{r}
s <- gr_scorer_answer()
item <- list(question = "How many units?", document = gr_example())
s$fn(item, "Leeds made 12,400 units.", "12400")$correct
s$fn(item, "Leeds made 112,400 units.", "12400")$correct
s$fn(item, "Revenue was 45.2 million dollars.", "12400")$failure_kind
```

On an unanswerable item it is right when `is_not_found()` is `TRUE` and no limit
or refusal stopped the run, since a reader that ran out of budget did not look.
`hr_scorer()` makes a scorer of your own from a function of `(item, output,
label)`; its help has one that accepts a number within 1% of the label.

## Running a benchmark

`hr_benchmark()` runs every arm on every item of the chosen splits `runs`
times, scores each output, and returns one row per cluster, item, arm and run.
The stand-in model below knows each report's facts. Asked as `mock-small` it
loses its way on 30% of requests; as `mock-large` it does not:

```{r}
facts <- list(
  northern = c(revenue = "Revenue was 45.2 million dollars.", units = "Leeds made 12,400 units."),
  southern = c(revenue = "Revenue was 51.8 million dollars.", staff = "There were 310 staff."),
  eastern  = c(revenue = "Revenue was 38.9 million dollars."),
  western  = c(revenue = "Revenue was 29.4 million dollars.", exports = "Exports rose 7 percent."))

cl <- gr_mock_client(function(messages, params) {
  seen <- paste(vapply(messages, function(m) as.character(m$content), ""), collapse = " ")
  region <- regmatches(seen, regexpr("(northern|southern|eastern|western)", seen))
  asked <- sub(".*Question", "", seen)
  topic <- c("revenue", "units", "staff", "exports")
  hit <- topic[vapply(topic, grepl, logical(1), x = asked, ignore.case = TRUE)][1]
  reply <- facts[[region]][hit]
  if (is.na(reply)) return("NOT_IN_DOCUMENT")
  if (identical(params$model, "mock-small") && runif(1) < 0.3) return("The report is unclear.")
  reply
})

bench <- hr_benchmark(arms, qa, runs = 5, client = cl, scorer = gr_scorer_answer())
bench
head(bench[, c("item", "arm", "run", "correct", "failure_kind", "usd", "draw_index")])
```

The printed accuracy is the mean over runs within each item, then over items,
and is descriptive: no interval. The arms run under a private random stream
started from `seed` (1 by default), which is why the mock's `runif()` gives the
same draws every time this guide is built, and the caller's random state is
left as it was. Rows on the dev split are marked `reportable = FALSE` and
printed apart. Five runs is the default and the expected minimum; fewer warns
with class `hr_few_runs`, because with fewer the spread from run to run cannot
be told from the difference between arms.

### One limit for the whole benchmark

The benchmark is one run under one `hr_governor()`. Each run's trace is held to
the governor's limits less what the runs before it used, so the limit you set
is the most the whole comparison can spend. With `governor = NULL` the limits
come from `gr_options()`, whose default of 400 calls is easy to exceed: two arms
on 300 items for 5 runs is 3000 calls. A run stopped by a refused request is
recorded as a `"budget_stop"`, counted wrong, and the runs after it are still
started, so every row exists and the refusals are visible:

```{r}
capitals <- hr_reference(items = list(q1 = "France", q2 = "Peru", q3 = "Chad", q4 = "Fiji"),
                         labels = c("Paris", "Lima", "N'Djamena", "Suva"),
                         cluster = c("a", "a", "b", "b"), split = "test")
atlas <- c(France = "Paris", Peru = "Lima", Chad = "N'Djamena", Fiji = "Suva")
geo <- gr_mock_client(function(messages, params) atlas[[sub("Capital of ", "", messages[[1]]$content)]])
capital <- hr_arm("capital", function(item, ctx) ctx$call(paste0("Capital of ", item))$text)

short <- hr_benchmark(capital, capitals, runs = 5, client = geo,
                      governor = hr_governor(max_calls = 6))
table(short$failure_kind, useNA = "ifany")
```

The first six runs were answered, and the other fourteen were refused before
anything was sent.

### Repeated runs must be repeated draws

Run `r` is given `ctx$draw_index = r`, and `ctx$call()` passes it on, so under
a `gr_cache()` each run is its own cache entry and under a `gr_replay_client()`
its own recorded draw. Five runs answered from one stored reply would agree
perfectly and measure nothing, so an arm whose runs come back as copies is
refused with an error of class `hr_duplicate_draw`. An arm that calls
`gr_call()` without the draw index is one:

```{r}
cache <- gr_cache()
cached <- gr_cache_client(geo, cache)
invisible(hr_benchmark(capital, capitals, runs = 5, client = cached))

no_draw <- hr_arm("no_draw", function(item, ctx) {
  gr_call(ctx$client, paste0("Capital of ", item), trace = ctx$trace)$text
})
tryCatch(hr_benchmark(no_draw, capitals, runs = 5, client = cached),
         hr_duplicate_draw = function(e) class(e)[1])
```

A cache is still worth having: running the `capital` benchmark again under the
same cache sends no request and costs nothing, each run answered from its own
entry.
A `gr_mock_client()` keeps no cache, so under it the `no_draw` arm is not
refused; under a cache it is.

## Reading the report

`hr_report()` turns the reportable rows into accuracy per arm with intervals
that keep clusters together, paired differences, stability, reliability, cost
and failures. `B` is the number of cluster bootstrap resamples, 2000 by
default; this guide uses fewer so it builds quickly.

```{r}
rpt <- hr_report(bench, B = 200)
rpt
```

Which interval is used depends on the size of the benchmark, and the second
line of the print says which and why. With at least 300 items and at least 30
clusters, `method = "auto"` uses a studentised cluster bootstrap: each resample
draws whole clusters with all their items, runs and arms. Below either
threshold, as here, it uses a cluster-robust t interval on the logit scale,
with t quantiles on C - 1 degrees of freedom for C clusters. Where neither is
defined, because accuracy is 0 or 1 or the same in every cluster, the arm gets
Korn and Graubard's interval, one-sided from that bound; that is why `large`
reads [0.561, 1.000] with four clusters behind it, and a note says so. No
interval treats items or runs as independent trials. `method = "exact"`
(Clopper-Pearson on the effective number of items) and `method = "bayes"` (a
beta-binomial model with a cluster random effect) are there on request.

These defaults were chosen by simulation. In `dev/sim-coverage.R` (2000
replicates) the studentised bootstrap covered 95.5% and 95.0% with 386 items in
40 clusters, where the BCa bootstrap it replaced covered 93.5%, and the
cluster-robust t interval covered 95.7% and 95.8% with 50 items in 10 clusters.
The workflow `validation.yaml` reruns that simulation, and the one behind
`hr_mdd()`, every night.

Paired differences are taken item by item, so each one compares the arms on
the same question, with a cluster-robust t interval at every size and
simultaneous intervals over all pairs beside it. Arms are listed in benchmark
order, not ranked; the rank interval is how much the order could change over
resamples, and `small` and `large` here are ranked 2 and 1 in every one.

The stability rows describe each arm against itself. The flip rate is the share
of items whose correctness changed between runs, TARa the share whose scored
output was the same on every run, and `run_sd` the spread of whole-run accuracy.
`small` flips on 75% of its items, which an accuracy of 0.750 alone would hide.
Reliability is pass^k, the chance that k runs drawn from an item's runs are all
right, estimated without bias: an arm right 75% of the time is right on all
five runs of an item only 25% of the time here.

Cost is in dollars and tokens per item and per correct item, since a cheap arm
that is often wrong can cost more per right answer than it looks. An arm whose
dollars rest on estimated token counts for more than 5% of its spend is
flagged; the mock reports no token counts, so both are flagged here. The
frontier is the set of arms no other arm beats on both dollars per item and
accuracy, with each arm's share of resamples on it. Failures are counted by
kind, every one counted wrong, with accuracy recomputed without parse failures
and refusals beside it. The variance line splits the spread into within-item
(run to run) and between-item parts; when runs account for more than 10% of it,
as here at 80%, the report says to use 10 runs.

Below 5 runs the report is descriptive only, with point estimates and no
intervals. An item scored on some runs and not others is refused. Everything
is in the returned list (`rpt$accuracy`, `rpt$contrasts`, `rpt$pass_k`,
`rpt$cost`, `rpt$frontier`, `rpt$failures`, `rpt$variance`, `rpt$notes`), and
`as_json()` writes it out.

## Planning the size, and non-inferiority

Often the question is whether a cheaper arm is worse than the one in use by
more than a margin you can live with. That is a non-inferiority test. Whether a
benchmark can answer it depends on its size, which is worth knowing before
anyone labels 500 questions.

`hr_mdd()` gives the smallest paired difference a clustered design can detect.
It needs the number of items and clusters, the intra-cluster correlation of the
paired item difference (ICC_D, taken from a pilot on the dev split) and the
share of items on which the arms disagree (`p_disc`). For 480 questions over 80
documents:

```{r}
hr_mdd(480, n_clusters = 80, icc = 0.2, p_disc = 0.2)
hr_mdd(480, n_clusters = 80, icc = 0.2, p_disc = 0.2, n_contrasts = 9)
```

Questions in one document count for less than independent ones: the design
effect DE = 1 + (m - 1) x ICC_D is 2 here, so 480 questions carry the
information of 240. With nine confirmatory contrasts, Holm's first step tests
at 0.025 / 9, and the detectable difference grows from 8.2 to 10.7 points.
`hr_n_needed()` turns it round, giving the items needed for a margin:

```{r}
hr_n_needed(0.08, m = 6, icc = 0.2, p_disc = 0.2, n_contrasts = 9)
```

Both use t quantiles on C - 1 degrees of freedom, the ones the report tests
with. In the power simulation `dev/sim-power.R` the formula's MDD was within
0.25 points of the simulated one; with normal quantiles it was up to 0.41
points below it at 80 clusters, which is why t quantiles are used.

`hr_contrast()` states a contrast (the new arm, the reference arm, the margin
and whether the new arm must also be cheaper) and `hr_register_contrasts()`
fixes the contrasts against the reference before anything scores it. The help
suggests a margin of min(0.5 x M1, the loss you would accept in practice), with
M1 the reference arm's advantage over a minimal baseline in a pilot. A
confirmatory margin below the design's MDD after Holm is refused with class
`hr_margin_below_mdd`, since it claims more than the items can show;
`confirmatory = FALSE` registers it as exploratory instead. A reference a
benchmark has already begun to score is refused with class
`hr_registration_after_scoring`.

```{r}
n <- 300
ids <- sprintf("q%03d", 1:n)
docs <- rep(sprintf("doc%02d", 1:50), each = 6)
plan <- hr_reference(ids, labels = rep("yes", n), cluster = docs, split = "test")

design <- hr_mdd(n, n_clusters = 50, icc = 0.1, p_disc = 0.15)
reg <- hr_register_contrasts(plan, hr_contrast("small", "large", margin = 0.10), design)
reg
```

Here the stand-in model finds each item easier or harder by document and by
item, and `mock-small` is a little worse on every one. The governor allows the
3000 calls the benchmark needs:

```{r}
set.seed(11)
ease <- setNames(rnorm(50, 2, 1)[as.integer(factor(docs))] + rnorm(n, 0, 1.5), ids)
grader <- gr_mock_client(function(messages, params) {
  shift <- if (identical(params$model, "mock-small")) -0.3 else 0
  item <- sub("Item ", "", messages[[1]]$content)
  if (runif(1) < plogis(ease[[item]] + shift)) "yes" else "no"
})

trial <- hr_benchmark(list(ask("large", "mock-large"), ask("small", "mock-small")),
                      plan, runs = 5, client = grader,
                      governor = hr_governor(max_calls = 4000, max_cost_usd = 1))
ni <- hr_report(trial, B = 500, registration = reg)
ni$method_reason
ni$ni[, c("new", "reference", "margin", "estimate", "lower", "cost_upper",
          "verdict", "mdd_design", "mdd_achieved")]
```

With 300 items in 50 clusters the report switches to the studentised bootstrap.
A contrast holds only if the one-sided lower bound of the accuracy difference is
above -margin and, with the cost test, the upper bound of the paired cost
difference is below 0. Here `small` is 5.3 points less accurate than `large`,
its lower bound is -8.1 points, inside the margin of 10, and its cost bound is
below 0, so the verdict is `TRUE`. The accuracy bound is the cluster-robust t
bound of the paired differences, so at one-sided 0.025 it is the lower end of
the printed 95% contrast interval. Confirmatory contrasts are tested with Holm's
step-down procedure. The design and achieved MDD are printed beside the verdict,
and Tango's paired score interval sits beside it as a cross-check that does not
enter the verdict.

A report with a registration, or with `confirmatory = TRUE`, is evidence, so
any row from the dev, exploratory or calibration split is refused with class
`hr_dev_not_evidence`, and so is a registration edited after it was made.

## Judges

Some answers cannot be scored by matching text: a summary, an explanation, an
answer that is right in other words. `hr_judge()` asks a model to choose
between candidates (`"select"`), compare two (`"pairwise"`) or grade one
against a reference (`"grade"`). Candidates are shown under the letters A, B
and so on, never their names, and each item is asked in two orders. A verdict
that changes with the order, mapped back to the candidate it names, is
`"unresolved"`, never a pick. This stand-in always picks whatever is shown
first:

```{r}
first <- gr_mock_client(function(messages, params) '{"verdict": "A", "reason": "It is first."}')
j <- hr_judge(c(short = "Revenue was 45.2 million.", long = "Revenue was 51.8 million."),
              first, mode = "select", rubric = "Which candidate gives fiscal 2024 revenue?")
j$outcome
j$verdicts[, c("order", "shown", "verdict", "value")]
```

The judge's requests go through the same check as `gr_call()`, under the
labels `judge.<mode>.o<k>`, into a trace of the judge's own. Their cost is in
`j$judge_cost` and never in the trace of the run being judged.

`hr_judge_config()` holds everything that decides a judge's answers (model,
mode, rubric, the package's instructions, reply schema, orders, how verdicts
are combined, the positive grade) with a hash of it. `hr_judge_validate()`
compares the judge's decisions with blind human labels for one configuration.
It refuses fewer than 50 human-positive or 50 human-negative items, with class
`hr_judge_too_few_labels`, and the minimums cannot be lowered: at 10%
prevalence, 100 labels hold 10 positives and a sensitivity interval of about
plus or minus 0.3. The judge's decisions here are simulated as right 90% of the
time:

```{r}
gr_register_model("mock-judge", context_window = 128000, max_output = 4096,
                  input_usd = 1, output_usd = 4)
cfg <- hr_judge_config("mock-judge", "Does the response give the reference's answer?",
                       mode = "grade")

set.seed(3)
human <- rep(c(TRUE, FALSE), c(60, 60))
judged <- ifelse(runif(120) < 0.9, human, !human)
judged[c(5, 70)] <- NA       # unresolved by the judge
v <- hr_judge_validate(cfg, data.frame(judge = judged, human = human), B = 200)
v
```

Items the judge left unresolved count as not called positive, which is how the
scorer will count them, so the figures describe the judge as it will be used.
Whether they are good enough for your purpose is a decision to make before
labelling; the function measures and does not admit. The record is keyed by the
configuration's hash, and `hr_judge_valid()` says when it no longer holds:

```{r}
hr_judge_valid(v, cfg)
hr_judge_valid(v, hr_judge_config("mock-judge", "Is the response right?", mode = "grade"))
```

`hr_scorer_judge()` is a benchmark scorer that grades each output against its
label with a grade-mode judge. It refuses to be built without a valid record
(class `hr_judge_unvalidated`). An unresolved judgement counts as wrong and a
failed one as an error, so an arm's accuracy cannot rise on the items the judge
could not settle, and the judge's requests stay in the scorer's own trace, out
of the benchmark's cost columns:

```{r}
grader_judge <- gr_mock_client(function(messages, params) {
  shown <- sub(".*Response to grade:", "", messages[[2]]$content)
  ok <- grepl("45.2 million", shown, fixed = TRUE)
  sprintf('{"verdict": "%s", "reason": "Compared."}', if (ok) "pass" else "fail")
})
judge_scorer <- hr_scorer_judge(cfg, v, grader_judge)
judge_scorer$fn("What was revenue?", "It came to 45.2 million dollars.", "45.2 million")$correct
```

A judge's accuracy figures carry its own errors. `hr_judge_ppi()` corrects
judge-scored accuracy with human labels on a sample, by prediction-powered
inference (PPI++ by default). Here a lenient judge passes 30% of wrong answers
on 1000 items, and people label 150 of them:

```{r}
set.seed(7)
truth <- rbinom(1000, 1, 0.6)
lenient <- ifelse(truth == 1, rbinom(1000, 1, 0.95), rbinom(1000, 1, 0.3))
labelled <- rep(NA, 1000)
picked <- sample(1000, 150)
labelled[picked] <- truth[picked]
hr_judge_ppi(lenient, labelled)[, c("estimate", "lower", "upper", "judge_mean")]
mean(truth)
```

The judge alone says 0.698. Corrected with the 150 labels the estimate is 0.567,
and its interval, 0.505 to 0.628, holds the true share of 0.594. When the
labelled items were drawn with unequal probabilities, pass `inclusion_prob` and
the correction is inverse probability weighted. The interval is a normal
approximation and runs narrow with few labels at small inclusion probabilities.

## Baselines without a model

A configuration that calls a model should beat one that does not.
`hr_baseline_classifier()` fits a ridge logistic regression on tf-idf features
(`hr_tfidf()`) and cross-fits it, so every item is predicted by a model that
never saw it, with the vocabulary fitted on each training fold only. Folds are
stratified by label, or keep each `cluster` whole:

```{r}
set.seed(1)
words <- function(pool, n) vapply(seq_len(n), function(i) paste(sample(pool, 6, TRUE), collapse = " "), "")
abstracts <- c(words(c("masks", "infection", "trial", "ward", "virus"), 10),
               words(c("budget", "policy", "school", "survey", "income"), 50))
relevant <- rep(c(TRUE, FALSE), c(10, 50))

hr_baseline_classifier(abstracts, relevant, folds = 5)
```

Real abstracts do not separate this cleanly. Run the baseline on the same
labelled set as the model screener: a screener no more accurate than it costs
calls and buys nothing.

`hr_baseline_ranker()` simulates prioritised screening over a set whose
relevance is known, as ASReview's simulation mode does: it starts from one
relevant and one irrelevant record, refits after each batch, and screens the
record with the highest predicted relevance next. It reports the records
screened to reach 95% recall and WSS@95, the share left unread at that recall
less the 5% a random order would leave:

```{r}
ranked <- hr_baseline_ranker(abstracts, relevant)
ranked
```

`gr_stop_test()` takes this result, or any screening order, and says when
prioritised screening may stop; `vignette("review")` covers it.

## Drift

A provider can change a model behind the same name. `hr_drift_check()` reruns
an arm live on the items of a frozen benchmark and compares the two item by
item, with `alpha` and an optional `alert` fixed in the call before anything is
rerun. Here the model has since learned two capitals wrong:

```{r}
six <- hr_reference(
  items = list(q1 = "France", q2 = "Peru", q3 = "Chad", q4 = "Fiji", q5 = "Chile", q6 = "Laos"),
  labels = c("Paris", "Lima", "N'Djamena", "Suva", "Santiago", "Vientiane"),
  cluster = c("a", "a", "b", "b", "c", "c"), split = "test")
then <- c(France = "Paris", Peru = "Lima", Chad = "N'Djamena", Fiji = "Suva",
          Chile = "Santiago", Laos = "Vientiane")
now <- then
now[c("Chad", "Laos")] <- c("Ndjamena", "Luang Prabang")
answers <- function(table) {
  gr_mock_client(function(messages, params) table[[sub("Capital of ", "", messages[[1]]$content)]])
}

frozen <- hr_benchmark(capital, six, runs = 5, client = answers(then))
drift <- hr_drift_check(frozen, capital, client = answers(now), reference = six,
                        alert = 0.1, B = 500)
drift
```

Test (a) is the change in accuracy, live minus frozen, by a cluster bootstrap
over documents, with the clustered McNemar test beside it. Test (b) asks
whether frozen and live runs disagree more than replicate runs disagree among
themselves; per item it estimates the squared change, so it also sees losses
and gains that cancel in accuracy. Here (a) finds the two lost items, a change
of -0.333 with an interval that lies wholly beyond the alert of 0.1. Test (b)
does not reject: with three clusters its one-sided bound reaches 0. The live
rerun is in `drift$live`, an `hr_bench` you can report or keep as the next
frozen sample. Fewer than 5 frozen runs, a changed
arm, another reference or scorer, and a live rerun answered from a cache or a
recording are refused: that last one would be the frozen reply again, not the
model today.

## Signals, calibration and gate thresholds

Some readers report on their own work: the `iterative` reader says at each step
whether it can answer, `preview` says which sections its plan would skip, and
`ensemble` says how it settled its members. `hr_signal()` records such a value
as a local step in the trace, which sends no request and changes no cache key,
and `hr_signals()` reads them back:

```{r}
reader <- gr_mock_client(function(m, p) {
  '{"can_answer": true, "answer": "45.2 million dollars", "next_query": ""}'
})
ch <- gr_segment(gr_example(), list(method = "sentence", max_tokens = 150))
read <- gr_read(ch, "What was revenue?", reader, "iterative")
hr_signals(read)[, c("signal", "value", "score", "refs")]
```

A signal is advisory. Nothing in the package acts on one, and a signal may
gate an action only after it has been measured against items whose right
answer is known. `hr_calibrate_signal()` does that on a graded set, which must
include unanswerable items: a signal measured only on answerable questions has
never been asked about the case where "I can answer" is most often wrong. It
fits a map from the signal to a probability on half of each cluster's items
and measures it on the other half, with the Brier score, type-2 AUROC, the area
under the risk-coverage curve and a debiased calibration error, each with a
cluster bootstrap interval. The record is keyed by the served model, its
version, the task, format, prompt hash, effort, module and contract version.
The graded set here is simulated, 1200 items in 120 documents:

```{r}
set.seed(2)
n <- 1200
answerable <- runif(n) < 0.8
score <- runif(n) * ifelse(answerable, 1, 0.6)
graded <- data.frame(cluster = rep(sprintf("doc%03d", 1:120), each = 10),
                     score = score, answerable = answerable,
                     correct = runif(n) < plogis(-6 + 12 * score) / ifelse(answerable, 1, 3))
key <- list(served_model = "mock-large-2026-01", version = "2026-01", task = "qa",
            format = "txt", prompt_hash = "a1b2c3", effort = NA, module = "iterative")

cal <- hr_calibrate_signal("gr.iterative.can_answer", graded, key, seed = 3, B = 200)
cal
```

A new record is always advisory. `hr_gate_threshold()` looks for the loosest
threshold at which acting on the items at or above it keeps a risk below
`alpha` with confidence 1 - `delta`, by Learn-then-Test: thresholds are tested
from strict to loose with a one-sided Clopper-Pearson bound, and the sequence
stops at the first that fails. `alpha` has no default, since it is a decision
about the task:

```{r}
cal <- hr_gate_threshold(cal, "stop", alpha = 0.1)
as.data.frame(cal$gate[c("threshold", "n", "k", "ucb", "coverage", "status")])
cal$status
```

At the threshold kept, 147 items of the calibration half are acted on, 7 of
them wrongly, and the upper bound on the error among them is 0.088. A record
becomes `"gating"` only with a passing threshold, at least 100 wrong items in
the graded set, a map that rises with the signal and a calibration error over
at least 5 bins. Even then the signal gates only through a policy, and only for
a run whose key matches the record:

```{r}
policy <- hr_signal_policy("gr.iterative.can_answer", "stop")
hr_apply_signal(c(0.95, 0.4), policy, cal, key)[, c("value", "p", "gated", "act", "route")]

later <- utils::modifyList(key, list(served_model = "mock-large-2026-06"))
hr_calibration_valid(cal, later)
hr_apply_signal(0.95, policy, cal, later)$reason
```

When the signal cannot gate, the item is routed by `on_fail`: to a check (the
default), to a person, or nowhere. No reader calls `hr_apply_signal()` yet, so
in this release nothing gates on a signal.

## The statistics underneath

The functions above rest on five that can be used on their own.

`hr_prop_ci()` gives Wilson, Clopper-Pearson or Jeffreys intervals for a
proportion. Use Wilson for a descriptive rate and Clopper-Pearson for an "at
least" or "at most" claim, read as a one-sided bound:

```{r}
hr_prop_ci(46, 50)[, c("est", "lower", "upper", "method")]
hr_prop_ci(46, 50, method = "clopper_pearson", side = "lower")[, c("lower", "method", "side")]
```

`hr_agreement()` reports agreement between two raters as the count table with
observed agreement, Cohen's kappa with a bootstrap interval, the prevalence and
bias indices, PABAK, Gwet's AC1, and sensitivity, specificity, PPV and NPV when
`positive` is given. Kappa is never reported alone, since it moves with
prevalence as much as with agreement. For a matrix of coders, or an ordinal,
interval or ratio level, it reports Krippendorff's alpha instead, and only
percent agreement below 30 items.

```{r}
screener <- rep(c("keep", "drop", "keep", "drop"), c(40, 9, 6, 45))
person   <- rep(c("keep", "keep", "drop", "drop"), c(40, 9, 6, 45))
hr_agreement(screener, person, positive = "keep", B = 200)$stats[1:4, ]
```

`hr_ht_estimate()` estimates a total, a mean or a ratio from a sample drawn
with known inclusion probabilities, optionally by stratum; it is how screening
recall is weighted on a stacked reference. `hr_ppi()` is the prediction-powered
estimate behind `hr_judge_ppi()`. `hr_alt_test()` runs the alternative
annotator test of Calderon, Reichart and Dror (2025), which asks whether a
model's labels can stand in for those of three or more people, with the margin
set by the people's declared expertise (`expertise` has no default):

```{r}
set.seed(3)
gold <- sample(c("a", "b", "c"), 80, replace = TRUE)
noisy <- function(p) ifelse(runif(80) < p, gold, sample(c("a", "b", "c"), 80, TRUE))
people <- sapply(1:4, function(j) noisy(0.75))
alt <- hr_alt_test(noisy(0.95), people, expertise = "skilled")
alt$omega
alt$passed
```

The model here wins against each of the four annotators, so the winning rate
omega is 1 and the test passes; it needs at least 30 items with two or more
human labels, and warns below 50.

```{r include = FALSE}
gr_options(old)
```
